title: Cab Booking System — LLD
summary: Class design for riders, drivers, and trips, with the real interview payoff: matching a rider to a driver whose location keeps changing, without scanning every driver.

slides.markdown:
The LLD version of "design Uber" drops the proximity-service, geo-partitioning, and map-routing internals that dominate the HLD answer, and asks you to get one thing right: the classes for `Rider`, `Driver`, and `Trip`, and the logic that matches a rider to a nearby available driver correctly under constant movement.

Treat map routing and ETA computation as an external black-box service you call, not something you design here. The interview payoff is entirely in the matching and trip-lifecycle logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: what's in scope, what isn't
slides.markdown:
**In scope:** riders request a trip from a pickup to a drop location; the system matches them to an available nearby driver; a trip moves through a lifecycle from request to completion; a fare is calculated at the end.

**Explicitly out of scope:** the internals of map routing and turn-by-turn navigation, and the distributed proximity-index architecture (that's the HLD question's territory). Here, assume a `LocationService.nearbyDrivers(point, radius)` call exists and focus on what happens with its results.

Naming this boundary early keeps you from re-deriving a geospatial index from scratch when the interviewer wants to see matching and trip-state logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Rider, Driver, Trip, Location, FareCalculator
slides.markdown:
`Rider` and `Driver` are both users with a role; `Driver` additionally carries an availability flag and a current `Location` that updates on every location ping. `Trip` is the central entity — it references a rider, a driver (once matched), pickup/drop locations, a status, and timestamps for each state transition.

`FareCalculator` is deliberately separate from `Trip`: fare depends on distance, time, and pricing rules that change independently of trip logic, so `Trip` asks `FareCalculator.calculate(trip)` rather than computing fare inline.

Keeping `Location` as its own value object (not just lat/lng fields scattered across classes) makes it easy to swap in a real geospatial index later without touching `Rider` or `Driver`.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: finding the nearest available driver
The hard part: matching under constant driver-location churn
slides.markdown:
Every available driver sends a location ping every few seconds. With 10,000 drivers in a city, that's a high write rate against whatever structure tracks positions — and a naive design that scans every driver's row to compute distance on each match request turns an O(1)-feeling lookup into an O(n) scan repeated for every rider request.

The fix is a spatial index — a grid (geohash buckets) or a quadtree — that drivers update on each ping (cheap, localized write) and that `nearby(point, radius)` queries in roughly O(log n) or better by only touching nearby cells, not the whole driver set.

The interview signal here isn't "use a geospatial index" as a buzzword — it's explaining why a write-heavy, read-heavy workload on the same data needs an index structure that keeps both cheap.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: greedy nearest-driver matching vs batched assignment
slides.markdown:
Greedy matching assigns the nearest available driver to each request the instant it arrives. Batched matching collects requests and drivers over a short window (a few seconds) and solves the assignment jointly.

| | Greedy (immediate) | Batched assignment |
|---|---|---|
| Rider wait to get matched | Near-zero | Up to the batch window |
| Total pickup distance across all trips | Can be far from optimal | Lower — solved jointly |
| Complexity | Simple, one comparison per request | Needs a matching/optimization step |
| Best fit | Low-density areas, sparse drivers | Dense areas at peak (many requests, many drivers) |

**How to decide:** greedy is the right default — it's simpler and rider-latency-sensitive. Reach for batching only where request density is high enough that joint optimization measurably cuts total pickup distance, like a downtown core at rush hour.

slides.sectionTitle: Surge pricing as a strategy consulted at request time
slides.markdown:
Surge pricing depends on live supply and demand in an area — a ratio of open requests to available drivers — and that ratio changes by the minute. Hardcoding a multiplier into `FareCalculator` means every pricing experiment is a code change to core fare logic.

Instead, `FareCalculator` consults a `PricingStrategy` at request time — a `SurgePricingStrategy` computes a multiplier from current supply/demand, while a `FlatPricingStrategy` returns 1.0. This is the same Strategy shape used for seat pricing in the movie-booking case: an interface the calculator calls, swappable without touching the calculator itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: two riders' requests matching to the same driver
slides.markdown:
Two riders near the same driver both call `findNearestDriver` within the same tens of milliseconds; both get the same driver back, since neither request has claimed anything yet — `findNearestDriver` only reads.

The fix is the same shape as seat holding: claiming a driver must be an atomic conditional write, not a separate step after the read — `UPDATE drivers SET status='MATCHED', trip_id=? WHERE driver_id=? AND status='AVAILABLE'`. Whichever request's update actually changes a row wins; the loser's matching service immediately re-queries for the next-nearest available driver instead of failing the rider outright.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: recomputing a full driver search on every location ping
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Keep it simple — on every driver location ping, just re-scan all drivers to keep an in-memory list sorted by area."

**Why it's wrong:** location pings arrive continuously from every driver, far more often than match requests happen. Doing an O(n) re-sort or re-scan on every single ping means the system's cost scales with driver count times ping frequency — it gets slower exactly as the fleet you're trying to serve grows.

**Correct model:** pings should be cheap, localized index updates (move this one driver's entry in a grid/quadtree cell), and the expensive nearby-search work should happen only when a match request actually needs it — read and write paths should have very different costs on the same structure.
